newsitem.title: FRANCE: French political foes scramble to stop far-right.
newsitem.headline: French political foes scramble to stop far-right.

text.p: France's centre-right and Socialist parties scrambled on Monday to stop the far-right National Front conquering a fourth town in municipal elections, uniting behind a single "republican" candidate.

The anti-immigrant Front's Catherine Megret triumphed in the first round of a fiercely-contested poll in Vitrolles near Marseille at the weekend, prompting the government candidate to pull out of next Sunday's run-off after being pressed to do so by heavyweights including Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

"I urge the citizens of Vitrolles to adopt a republican attitude and vote as their souls and consciences tell them to do," centre-right candidate Roger Guichard told a news conference in announcing his decision to drop out of the race.

"What we all want is the list of the (centre-right) candidate which came third to pull out." Juppe had told France Inter radio earlier in the day, urging his supporters to unite behind the Socialists in the run-off.

The election is a test of the allure of the National Front ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections and amid record unemployment in France. Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen wants to send home millions of immigrants from third world states.

Stepping into the shoes of her husband -- Front deputy leader Bruno Megret -- after he was banned from running, Catherine Megret fell short of the 50 percent needed to be elected outright mayor of the depressed town of 39,000 people.
But she took 46.7 percent of the vote, ahead of outgoing Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade on 37.0 and centre-rightist Roger Guichard on 16.3 percent.
Socialist leaders had also urged Guichard to withdraw though there was some dissension within the governing centre-right.
Gaullist ex-Interior Minister Charles Pasqua urged government parties to steal basic values like patriotism back from the Front rather than drop out.
And a faction led by Foreign Minister Herve de Charette painted the choice between Megret and Anglade as a choice "between the plague and cholera".
Bruno Megret said Juppe covered himself in shame in supporting Anglade, "a candidate who has been invalidated, stripped of his post, and placed under investigation for forgery".
Some Socialists in Vitrolles apparently agreed, saying it was not too late to replace Anglade with a stronger candidate.
The Front, which has no seats in parliament, won control of its first three towns in France in nation-wide municipal elections in 1995 -- Marignane, Orange and Toulon.

In those elections, Anglade overturned a big Front first round lead to win the Vitrolles municipality on the second round by a wafer-thin 353 votes. But the vote was later cancelled because of irregularities by Anglade's camp.
Anglade called a rally for Wednesday to be attended by Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue.
Megret, beaten by Anglade in 1995, was banned from running this month for exceeding campaign spending limits. He chose instead to be "represented" by his wife, who has scant political experience.
Bruno Megret says he will be her chief adviser if she wins, and that Front policies of priority for white French people will help bring down the town's 19 percent unemployment.
